title: Tree Columns in Level Order
statement:
Draw a binary tree on a grid. The root is in column 0. A left child is one column to the left of its parent, and a right child one column to the right.

Return the node values grouped by column, from the leftmost column to the rightmost. Inside a column, list nodes from top to bottom. When two nodes share the same row and column, the one further left in that row comes first (the order a level-by-level walk meets them). Do not sort by value.

An empty tree gives [].

examples.why: 9 and 8 share row 2, column 0. 9 is further left, so it comes first even though it is larger.
5 hangs deep under the left subtree but lands in column 1, below 3. A depth-first walk would meet 5 before 3; rows must decide.

hints: Every node needs a column number. Carry it along as you visit nodes: the left child gets col − 1, the right child col + 1.
Which traversal already visits nodes top to bottom, and left to right within a row? Use it, and the order inside each column comes for free.
BFS with (node, col) pairs. Append each value to a map entry for its column, and track the smallest and largest column so you can output them in order without sorting.

explain.intuition:
The required order inside a column is "by row, then left to right". That is exactly the order a breadth-first walk visits nodes. So if you do BFS and append each value to its column's list as you meet it, every list is already in the right order.

Columns span a contiguous range from the leftmost to the rightmost, so track minCol and maxCol and read the map from one to the other. A depth-first walk can also work, but then you must record each node's row and sort by it, because DFS can reach a deep node before a shallow one in the same column.
steps: If the tree is empty, return [].
Start a queue with (root, 0) and an empty map from column to list.
Pop (node, col), append node.val to map[col], update minCol and maxCol, and push the children with col − 1 and col + 1 (left first).
pitfalls: Plain DFS without rows. In the second example it puts 5 before 3 in column 1.
Sorting ties by value. That is a different problem; here the left-to-right position decides.
Pushing the right child before the left, which flips the order of nodes that share a cell.

solutions.title: DFS with rows, then sort
solutions.idea: Record (col, row, visit index) for every node with a pre-order walk, sort, and group by column. Pre-order meets same-row nodes left to right, so the visit index breaks ties correctly.

solutions.title: BFS with a column map
solutions.idea: Breadth-first order is already top to bottom, left to right. Append to each column's list as you go and read columns from min to max.

followups: Inside a shared cell, sort by value instead. What is the cheapest change?
Return only the topmost node of each column (the view from above).
